title: Nimzo-Indian Defense: the pin on c3 and the plans around doubled pawns
outcomes: Names the first moves of the Nimzo-Indian (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4), what the bishop pins, and the structure after ...Bxc3 and bxc3 (bishop pair for White, doubled c-pawns)
Answers a3 by checking the retreats instead of keeping the bishop out of habit
As Black, adds attackers to the pawn on c4; as White, checks how many pieces attack e4 before advancing the e-pawn
Reads opening statistics as results of games with a stated source and sample size, not as evaluations

steps.text: **Nimzo-Indian Defense** (ECO E20 for the first position): 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4. The bishop pins the knight on c3 against the king, and the knight on f6 attacks e4. Black can later take on c3, which gives White the bishop pair and doubled c-pawns. This lesson covers the opening's plans only; the doubled-pawns and bishop lessons explain those ideas.

steps.caption: Position after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6, White to move. Step through one line with 4.a3. Other fourth moves are common; the next card shows which.

line.say: Nc3 develops a knight and attacks d5 and e4.
Bb4 pins the knight on c3 against the king.
a3 asks the bishop a question: the pawn attacks b4.
Bxc3+ takes the knight, with check.
bxc3 recaptures. White has two bishops and doubled pawns on c3 and c4.
c5 attacks d4 and starts play against the centre.
e3 supports d4 and opens the f1 bishop.
Nc6 adds a second attacker on d4.
Bd3 develops the bishop toward the kingside.
O-O puts the king in safety.
Ne2 develops the last knight and supports d4 and c3.
b6 prepares ...Ba6 against the pawn on c4.
e4 claims the centre and gives the bishops room.
Ne8 retreats the knight from f6.

claims.statement: After ...Bb4 the white knight on c3 has no legal move: it is pinned to the king.
The black knight on f6 attacks e4.
After a3 one white pawn attacks b4.
After bxc3 White's doubled pawns stand on c3 and c4.
After bxc3 only White has the bishop pair.
After ...b6 the bishop on c8 attacks a6, from where it would attack c4.
After e4 the pawn attacks d5 and f5.
After ...Ne8 the knight stands on e8.
At depth 16 the final position is within 0.6 pawn of level.

steps.text: **What strong players chose** (results of games, not evaluations). Our masters file: 329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more. After 3...Bb4 White played 4.e3 in 5,563 games (1,857 won by White, 2,349 drawn, 1,357 won by Black), 4.Qc2 in 3,501 (1,014, 1,725, 762), 4.f3 in 713 and 4.a3 in 384. Our online sample (Lichess Blitz, Rapid and Classical, 4,752,291 games, first 16 moves, all rating bands): 11,641 reach 3...Bb4, 2,203 reach 4.Qc2 and 1,786 reach 4.e3.

**White's plan (rule of thumb).** After ...Bxc3 and bxc3, White has two bishops and often advances e4 to open lines for them. Condition: count what attacks e4 first. Only the knight on f6 attacks it in the next position; an extra black attacker can turn the same advance into a lost pawn. Find the move, then compare the two cases.

**Black's plan (rule of thumb).** White's pawn on c4 has no b-pawn beside it, so only pieces can defend it. Black adds attackers: ...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Na5. In the masters data, after 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.bxc3, Black played ...c5 in 174 games, ...b6 in 88 and ...Nc6 in 42 (results of games, not evaluations). Condition: this asks White's pieces to defend; it wins nothing by itself.

**When the plans apply.** Both plans are rules of thumb for positions where Black has taken on c3 and White has recaptured with the b-pawn. Check that the structure is there: with the bishop still on b4 White has no doubled pawns. Then count attackers and defenders on the square you aim at. In the next three positions, only one feature differs.

steps.title: One knight moves, the central advance flips
steps.prompt: The first position is the one you already solved with e4. In all three positions White considers e4. Predict for each whether it is reasonable, then check. The first two differ only in where Black's queenside knight stands (c6 or d6). The third differs from the first only in where Black's h-pawn stands (h7 or h6).
Think about the positions you played without hints. Before you chose a move, what did you check? Write one line for each side.
